newsitem.title: KENYA: U.S. aid worker kidnapped in Somalia would return.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aid worker kidnapped in Somalia would return.

text.p: An American aid worker who escaped after being kidnapped by gunmen in Somalia said on Wednesday he would gladly return to the broken and violent Horn of Africa country to work.
Daniel Suther, 30, who worked with the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP), was kidnapped last Friday after renting a vehicle in Belet-Huen 260 km (160 miles) north of the capital Mogadishu.
Suther, who was also kidnapped last September, escaped the same day after jumping out of the vehicle and running into the desert. He was flown back to Nairobi from Belet-Huen on Sunday.

"We need to continue the work and we need to keep going back, so I am ready to go back," Suther, employed on the WFP programme by the U.S. Agency for International Development, told Reuters in an interview.
WFP working with other aid agencies completed on Tuesday a two-month programme to distribute emergency food aid to 300,000 Somalis vulnerable before the arrival of the main cereal harvest in August.

WFP distributed 3,240 tonnes of food packages, falling 650 tonnes short of its target. Distribution was halted in the Bay region when a Portuguese doctor with the aid agency Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF - Doctors Without Borders) was murdered at a hospital in Baidoa in June.

"Bullets, land mines and hard-to-get security clearances weren't our only obstacles. Washed out roads and the monsoon season made getting food shipments into the small seaside ports and then beyond an even tougher job," said WFP Somalia country director Burk Oberle.
Three men with just one weapon kidnapped Suther, a veteran of the country who speaks Somali, on Friday morning after they forced other passengers out of the vehicle en route to Tigieglo.
One kidnapper was a supporter of south Mogadishu faction leader Hussein Aideed, said Suther, originally from San Francisco, who first went to Somalia in 1990.
Militia loyal to Hussein Aideed's father Mohamed Farah Aideed fought U.S. and United Nations troops in Somalia under the banner of Operation Restore Hope during the famine.
Suther was kidnapped and released by Aideed supporters in Mogadishu last September.

The kidnappers last Friday headed south toward Mogadishu apparently intent on demanding a ransom and after four hours of driving and a shooting incident at a village, they stopped to allow three trucks to pass.
"When the second lorry came by I took off into the bush...I understood that he (the gunman) raised his weapon but the only shot he had was at the lorry," Suther said.
Suther headed west and then backtracked before spending a night in the open drinking nothing and eating dry acacia leaves.
He was rescued after meeting a camel driver who gave him water and tea and took him to a nearby village.
"With Somalis you get the worst and the best. When you are in trouble Somalis really come through and help you out," he said.
Somalia has been without central government since 1991 when President Mohamed Siad Barre was ousted. Hundreds of thousands died in 1992/93 in a famine and civil war.
Aid work has been drastically scaled down since March 1995 when the U.N. ended Operation Restore Hope, an aid mission backed by thousands of U.N. troops widely regarded as failure.
